:::{#def-quasi-newton-method}
#### Quasi-Newton method

Let $f : \reals^p \to \reals$ have first [partial derivatives](vector-calculus.qmd#def-partial-derivative),
let $\vx^{(0)}$ be a starting point,
and let $\matr{H}^{(0)}$ be a [positive definite matrix](linear-algebra.qmd#def-positive-definite).
A **quasi-Newton method**
[@nocedal2006numerical, Chapter 6]
produces, for $t = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$,

$$
\vx^{(t+1)} \eqdef \vx^{(t)} - s^{(t)} \matr{H}^{(t)} \deriv{\vx} f(\vx^{(t)}),
$$

where $s^{(t)} > 0$ is a [step length](#def-gradient-descent) chosen by a [line search](#def-line-search),
and $\matr{H}^{(t+1)}$ is a positive definite matrix
that satisfies the [secant condition](#def-secant-condition) in the form
$\matr{H}^{(t+1)} \vy^{(t)} = \vecf{s}^{(t)}$,
with $\vecf{s}^{(t)} = \vx^{(t+1)} - \vx^{(t)}$
and $\vy^{(t)} = \deriv{\vx} f(\vx^{(t+1)}) - \deriv{\vx} f(\vx^{(t)})$.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: {#exm-quasi-newton-step}
#### One quasi-Newton step on a quadratic function

Take $f(\vx) = \tfrac{1}{2} \qform{\matr{Q}}{\vx} - \dprod{\vecf{b}}{\vx}$
with $\matr{Q} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\vecf{b} = \tp{(1, 2)}$
(@exm-secant-condition),
$\vx^{(0)} = \vzero_{2 \times 1}$ and $\matr{H}^{(0)} = \matr{I}_2$.
For a [quadratic function](algebra-exponentials.qmd#def-quadratic-polynomial), the [step length](#def-gradient-descent) that minimizes $f$ along a [direction](vector-calculus.qmd#def-direction) $\vecf{d}$ is
$s = -\dprod{\deriv{\vx} f(\vx)}{\vecf{d}} / \qform{\matr{Q}}{\vecf{d}}$.

```{r}
#| label: quasi-newton-step
#| code-fold: false
Q <- matrix(c(4, 1, 1, 3), nrow = 2)
b <- c(1, 2)
f <- function(x) 0.5 * sum(x * (Q %*% x)) - sum(b * x)
grad <- function(x) drop(Q %*% x - b)
x0 <- c(0, 0)
H0 <- diag(2)
d <- -drop(H0 %*% grad(x0))
step <- -sum(grad(x0) * d) / drop(t(d) %*% Q %*% d)
x1 <- x0 + step * d
s <- x1 - x0
y <- grad(x1) - grad(x0)
```

The step length is `{r} step`, which moves the [iterate](#def-iterate) to $\vx^{(1)} = (`{r} x1[1]`, `{r} x1[2]`)$
and lowers $f$ from `{r} f(x0)` to `{r} f(x1)`.
Because $\matr{H}^{(0)} = \matr{I}_2$, this step is a [gradient descent](#def-gradient-descent) step.
The difference of the [gradients](vector-calculus.qmd#def-vector-derivative), $\vy^{(0)} = (`{r} y[1]`, `{r} y[2]`)$, is $\matr{Q} \vecf{s}^{(0)}$ ([the secant condition](#def-secant-condition) for a quadratic function).

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#rem-quasi-newton-cost}
#### Why a quasi-Newton method is used

Because $\matr{H}^{(t)}$ is [positive definite](linear-algebra.qmd#def-positive-definite), $-\matr{H}^{(t)} \deriv{\vx} f(\vx^{(t)})$ is a [descent direction](#def-descent-direction),
so a [line search](#def-line-search) finds a step that decreases $f$.
[Newton's method](#def-newton-method) needs the Hessian and the solution of a system of equations at every iteration,
which costs about $p^3$ operations for a dense $p \times p$ Hessian,
and requires the formulas for its entries.
A quasi-Newton method needs only the [gradient](vector-calculus.qmd#def-vector-derivative) and an update of $\matr{H}^{(t)}$ costing about $p^2$ operations.
Near a minimizer it is superlinearly fast: faster than [gradient descent](#def-gradient-descent), slower than Newton's method [@nocedal2006numerical, Chapter 6].
Replacing $\matr{H}^{(t)}$ by $\matr{I}_p$ in the step formula gives [gradient descent](#def-gradient-descent).

:::
